content: Uterus didelphys, also referred to as uterus didelphis, is a congenital uterine anomaly characterized by the presence of two separate uteri. This condition arises due to the failure of embryological fusion of the paired Müllerian ducts during development. As a result, each uterus is distinct and typically has a single horn connected to the corresponding fallopian tube and ovary on the same side. Etiology The uterus normally forms during embryogenesis through the fusion of the two Müllerian ducts into a single uterine cavity. In individuals with uterus didelphys, this fusion process does not occur, leading to the persistence of two separate Müllerian systems. This anomaly is often associated with a double cervix and, in many cases, a double vagina. The exact cause of the failure of fusion remains unknown. Additional defects may involve the vagina, renal system, and, less commonly, the skeletal system. Uterus didelphys is less common than other uterine malformations, such as arcuate uterus, septate uterus, and bicornuate uterus, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 3,000 women. Clinical Presentation Many women with uterus didelphys are asymptomatic and may remain unaware of the condition. However, a study by Heinonen involving 26 women with this anomaly revealed that gynecological complaints such as dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation) and dyspareunia (pain during intercourse) were common. All patients in the study exhibited a double vagina. Obstetric complications were also noted, with breech presentation occurring in 43% of cases and premature delivery in 21%. Diagnosis A pelvic examination often reveals the presence of a double vagina and double cervix, which may prompt further investigation. Diagnostic imaging techniques used to evaluate uterine structure include transvaginal ultrasonography, sonohysterography, hysterosalpingography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and hysteroscopy. More recently, three-dimensional ultrasonography has been advocated as a highly effective, non-invasive method for assessing uterine malformations. Management Women with uterus didelphys may require specialized care during pregnancy due to the increased risk of complications such as preterm birth and abnormal fetal presentation. Cesarean delivery is frequently necessary, with a reported rate of 82% in Heinonen's study. Associated Syndromes A specific syndrome involving uterus didelphys, unilateral hematocolpos (accumulation of menstrual blood in one vaginal canal), and ipsilateral renal agenesis (absence of a kidney on the same side) has been described. Multiple Pregnancies In rare cases, women with uterus didelphys can experience twin pregnancies, with each uterus carrying a separate pregnancy. Delivery may occur at different times, with intervals ranging from days to weeks. For example, a UK woman with uterus didelphys gave birth to triplets in 2006. Two of the triplets were identical twins resulting from a single egg implanted in one uterus, while the third baby developed from a separate egg implanted in the other uterus. The likelihood of such a birth is estimated to be approximately 1 in 25 million. Another case from Israel in 1981 reported a triplet pregnancy in a woman with uterus didelphys, where one baby died in utero, one was delivered at 27 weeks of gestation, and the third was delivered 72 days later.
